verdict.basis: Makatea was a single phosphate-mining island (annexed by France 1911) that was, for the entire 1908-1966 mining era, the ONLY source of phosphate rock exported from French Oceania/French Polynesia — there is no separate "French Polynesia total phosphate" series this label could be siphoning share from, so the sub-territory fold-up concern (Makatea's ~24km2 vs candidate's ~4000km2 land area) does not apply for this item: the parent is effectively the reporting unit because Makatea's output equals the territory's total phosphate output. The candidate wiki page (pyf-1800-2025.md, wiki_status: draft) is a bare CSV-derived stub — no mention of Makatea, phosphate, or any territorial reasoning at all, and it explicitly proxies a present-day GADM polygon across the entire 1800-2025 span pending review, which by itself rules out verified_equal for any assertion routed to this polity (French colonial acquisition of the various island groups was progressive through the 19th/early 20th century, so the reporting territory did not stay constant over so wide a span). Web cross-check (US Bureau of Mines Minerals Yearbook 1954) gives Makatea phosphate exports of ~247k long tons (1950) and ~252k long tons (1951), well above the bundle's median 92 thousand tonnes for 1949-1951 (n=6) — a ~2.5-3x gap that likely reflects a different weight basis (e.g. P2O5-equivalent nutrient content vs gross ore tonnage) rather than a territorial mismatch, since directionally the item is undeniably Makatea/French-Oceania phosphate in both sources.
verdict.wiki_note: Makatea was the sole phosphate-mining site in French Oceania/French Polynesia (mined 1908-1966 by Compagnie Française des Phosphates de l'Océanie), so despite naming a small island (~24km2) rather than the whole territory, this label carries French Polynesia's entire phosphate-rock output for the period — no other sub-unit shares or dilutes this reporting, so routing to the parent PYF polity is correct, not a fold-up error. Flag for future reference: FAO 1952 reports median ~92 thousand tonnes for 1949-1951, versus US Bureau of Mines (Minerals Yearbook 1954) figures of ~247k long tons (1950) and ~252k long tons (1951) for Makatea exports — a ~2.5-3x gap suggesting the FAO series may be on a P2O5-nutrient-equivalent basis rather than gross ore weight; this should be checked against other fao1952 phosphate rock entries before being treated as a settled convention.

review.wiki_note: Makatea is a small Tuamotu island (~24 km2) inside French Polynesia and would normally be a sub-territory fold-up risk, but during 1949-1951 Makatea was the SOLE phosphate-rock mining site in French Oceania (worked by Compagnie Française des Phosphates de l'Océanie), so 'Makatea' phosphate rock in an FAO/mining yearbook is effectively the entirety of French Polynesia's national phosphate output for this item, not a partial component of a much larger national total. Minerals Yearbook 1954 corroborates large-scale Makatea exports in this era (226k-252k long tons/yr for 1950-52), same order of magnitude as this source's figures, though not an exact match (possible rock-content vs gross-weight or export-vs-production differences). No standalone Makatea polity exists in the DB, and the candidate wiki page is a bare GADM-proxy stub that says nothing about Makatea, phosphate, or territorial scope -- it should be flagged for enrichment rather than relied on.
review.basis: Makatea's territory (a single small island) is far smaller than French Polynesia's overall national territory, which would normally trigger sub-territory fold-up (the exact 'Makatea inside French Polynesia' example given in the routing guidance). However, historical/mining literature confirms Makatea was the only phosphate-mining site in French Oceania/French Polynesia through this period, so the commodity total reported under the 'Makatea' label is, for this specific item, coextensive with the polity's entire national phosphate-rock output -- satisfying the 'parent IS the effective reporting unit for this item' exception. Magnitude (tens/hundreds of thousands of tonnes) is consistent with independently found Minerals Yearbook figures for Makatea exports in 1950-1952, though not an exact numeric match. Because Makatea's own territory is not generally equal to French Polynesia's (this only holds for the single-commodity phosphate case), this is best_available rather than verified_equal. The candidate wiki page is an uninformative draft stub (page_inadequate) that provides no independent corroboration.

verdict.basis: French Polynesia (former "Établissements français de l'Océanie") consolidated its constituent archipelagos (Society, Marquesas, Tuamotu-Gambier, Austral) under unified French colonial administration by 1903, after which its territorial extent has remained unchanged through the present day. The observed IIA data span (1909-1938) falls entirely within this stable post-1903 period, so there is no annexation/cession event to worry about within the span. The routed candidate PYF-1800-2025 uses a modern GADM adm0 polygon as proxy, which matches this same stable colonial/current territory. Staple magnitudes (tobacco ~22 ha, copra/other "p" ~39k tonnes, eggs 108t, sugar 200t, cacao 182 ha) are all consistent with a small Pacific island economy of this size, with no scale discontinuities suggesting a broader or narrower reporting unit. The wiki page itself is a thin draft stub (proxy polygon note only, no territorial history, area_km2 null) and does not itself support the verdict — it is being treated as an unreviewed hypothesis, not evidence.
verdict.wiki_note: Page is a thin proxy-polygon stub with no territorial history or area figure. External historical record: French Polynesia's constituent archipelagos (Society, Marquesas, Tuamotu-Gambier, Austral) were consolidated under unified colonial administration ("Établissements français de l'Océanie") by 1903 and the territory has not changed since — so the modern GADM proxy polygon is a valid stand-in for the 1909-1938 reporting territory, not just for the present day.

New Caledonia has been a distinct French colonial possession (annexed 1853) with unchanged territorial extent (the main island plus the Loyalty Islands and small dependencies) throughout the 1913-1945 span and up to today; IIA's 'New Caledonia' label is the colony reporting its own agricultural output, not a component folded into a larger French Pacific unit, so there is no sub-territory fold-up risk here.
verdict.basis: Assertion routes IIA rows labeled 'new caledonia' (iso ncl) 1913-1945 to NCL-1800-2025 by ISO match. The wiki page is a draft CSV-derived stub with no territorial documentation beyond a current-day GADM proxy polygon, so it cannot be leaned on directly (page_inadequate). However New Caledonia is itself the smallest administrative unit here (a French Pacific colony, not a province within a larger French colonial federation reported jointly), so the usual sub-territory fold-up failure does not apply: there is no larger 'French Pacific'/'French Oceania' aggregate this label could be a fraction of, and no separate historical New Caledonia predecessor/successor polity exists in the database to reroute to. Its colonial boundaries (Grande Terre plus Loyalty Islands and dependencies) were fixed by 1853 and did not change across 1913-1945 (no annexation, cession, or occupation event affecting New Caledonia in this period), satisfying the constant-territory requirement for verified_equal. Reported magnitudes (coffee green median 1,700 t, near-zero cotton, a fifth item 'p' at ~4,361 t) are plausible in scale for a small Pacific colony's agricultural/mineral output and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change. Confidence is medium rather than high because the thin wiki page and empty neighbor_segments mean the confirmation rests mainly on general historical knowledge of New Caledonia's colonial status rather than a dedicated external source consulted specifically for this task.

review.basis: New Caledonia was a distinct French colony (annexed 1853, comprising the main island, the Loyalty Islands, and the Isle of Pines) administered separately from other French Pacific possessions (French Polynesia / Établissements français de l'Océanie, New Hebrides condominium) throughout 1913-1945, with no annexations, cessions, or reorganizations affecting its borders in this span. IIA (International Institute of Agriculture), the pre-FAO statistical body, reported colonial agricultural output by individual colony, so "New Caledonia" as a label maps cleanly to this single stable reporting territory — no union/empire fold-up (unlike Australia/NZ dependencies elsewhere) and no combined-reporting risk with a sibling territory. The reported magnitudes (coffee ~1,700 t median, negligible cotton) are plausible for a small Pacific colonial economy of this era and show no step-change suggesting a scope shift. The wiki page itself is a thin, unreviewed draft (GADM current-polygon proxy, no historical boundary discussion) and cannot be relied on as evidence — it is flagged as page_inadequate — but the territorial continuity is independently supported by general historical knowledge of French Pacific colonial administration, not by the page's claims.
review.wiki_note: Page is a bare CSV-derived stub with no historical territorial discussion beyond a proxy-polygon note; it does not document that New Caledonia was administered separately from French Polynesia/New Hebrides throughout this period, which is the fact that actually supports treating it as a stable, distinct reporting unit for IIA colonial statistics.

verdict.basis: American Samoa is a small (~199 km²), US-administered island group whose territorial extent (Tutuila, Manu'a islands annexed 1904, Swains Island annexed 1925) was fixed well before the 1930-1934 observed span and unchanged through it -- no annexation, cession, or union-scope issue applies (unlike e.g. Samoa/Western Samoa, which the wiki correctly notes is a distinct, separate polity WSM-1900-2025). The IIA label 'american samoa' names the same small colonial territory, not a sub-component of something larger nor a combined-reporting label. The staple magnitude (tobacco, unmanufactured, median 54 ha across 12 rows/5 years) is plausible in scale for a ~199 km² island territory and shows no discontinuity suggesting a territorial-scope change. The wiki page is draft (unreviewed) but its specific factual claims -- area, distinctness from Samoa, 1925 boundary stability -- are independently plausible and consistent with known US-Samoa territorial history, so I treat them as corroborated rather than circularly cited.

French Somaliland (colonial Djibouti) is a distinct single-colony label with no union/empire ambiguity (unlike Sweden-Norway or Austria-Hungary cases) and no plausible sub-territory fold-up or combined-reporting risk. The wiki page (draft, thin/CSV-derived) states borders were fixed by the 1897 Franco-Ethiopian treaty and the polygon (CShapes 522, ~23,192 km2) is stable from 1900 through the colonial period, so the reporting territory did not change across the observed 1936-1951 span. FAO 1952 livestock magnitudes (goats 200k, sheep 100k, camels 3k, milk 8k tonnes, horses/mules/asses 6k) are plausible for this small, semi-arid, pastoral colony and show no scale discontinuity suggesting a broader or narrower reporting unit. No neighbor_segments data to cross-check, but nothing in the assertion suggests a mismatch. Verdict: confirm, verified_equal given the fixed, unchanged territory across the whole span.

review.basis: French Somaliland (colonial Djibouti) is a straightforward single-territory colony with no union, no combined-reporting, and no sub-territory fold-up risk — it's already the smallest administrative unit at this level. The candidate's area (23,192 km2, CShapes vintage 1900) matches present-day Djibouti's actual area (~23,200 km2), and the polity's borders were fixed by the 1897 Franco-Ethiopian treaty and held constant for the entire 1884-1977 span, well before and after the 1936-1951 observation window — so no boundary-vintage mismatch is plausible. The FAO 1952 yearbook's "French Somaliland" label is the standard name for this exact colonial administrative unit; there is no larger or smaller entity it could plausibly be confused with (it was never merged into a wider French Somali federation with different borders, and it is not a sub-unit of a larger reporting territory — it is itself the smallest coherent French colonial unit in the Horn of Africa). Staple magnitudes (goats ~200k, sheep ~100k, camels ~3k head, milk ~8k tonnes) are consistent order-of-magnitude for a small arid pastoralist territory of this size, and there is no red flag (no anomalously large step matching a much bigger neighboring territory like French West Africa or Ethiopia). The wiki page is draft-status but its core claim (fixed colonial borders since 1897, ~23,192 km2) is independently corroborable via well-documented history of Djibouti's colonial borders and its present-day area, so I am not relying on it circularly.

verdict.basis: The label 'djibouti' in IIA (1929-1945) routes to French Somaliland (FRS-1884-1977), whose borders were fixed by the 1897 Franco-Ethiopian treaty and did not change across the observed span, so the reporting territory (the French colonial customs/port jurisdiction of Djibouti) stayed constant and equals the candidate's territory for the whole span -- no annexation, cession, or split occurred 1929-1945. However, the magnitude is a red flag on its face: median 14,114 tonnes of green coffee is implausible as domestic production for an arid ~23,192 km2 territory with essentially no coffee agriculture. Web research confirms the resolution: the Djibouti-Addis Ababa railway (completed 1917) made the port of Djibouti the premier export outlet for Ethiopian highland coffee grown around Harar/southern Ethiopia, with France holding a de facto trade monopoly on Ethiopia's export route through the mid-1950s. So these IIA figures reflect coffee physically transiting/exported through French Somaliland's port (the correct reporting unit for that trade statistic), not coffee grown within its own territory. The territorial routing to FRS-1884-1977 is therefore correct (the customs point genuinely sits in this polity), but the data represents re-export/entrepot trade of a good produced elsewhere (Ethiopia), not domestic agricultural output -- a caveat worth recording since the wiki page is silent on the polity's economy entirely.
verdict.wiki_note: IIA 'coffee, green' figures for Djibouti/French Somaliland (median ~14,114 t/yr, 1929-1945) almost certainly reflect Ethiopian coffee (grown around Harar/southern Ethiopia) transiting the port via the Djibouti-Addis Ababa railway (completed 1917), not domestic production -- French Somaliland's arid terrain supports essentially no coffee cultivation. France held a de facto monopoly on Ethiopia's export trade through this port until Assab port opened in the mid-1950s. Flag this as re-export/entrepot trade, not production, to avoid double-counting against Ethiopia's own production series.

source_convention.convention: IIA figures reported under 'Djibouti'/French Somaliland for coffee, green are transit/re-export volumes of Ethiopian-origin coffee passing through the port via the Djibouti-Addis Ababa railway, not domestic production of the territory.
source_convention.evidence: Web research: the Djibouti-Addis Ababa railway (1897-1917) made Djibouti the premier export port for Ethiopian coffee from the Harar region; France held a near-monopoly on Ethiopia's export trade via this route until the mid-1950s. Magnitude (median 14,114 t/yr) is implausible as domestic output for a small arid territory with no known coffee agriculture.

verdict.basis: The known failure mode here is combined reporting (Territory of New Guinea + Territory of Papua were administered separately until their 1949 merger into the Territory of Papua and New Guinea). External web research on 1941 Australian administrative records gives Territory of New Guinea population ≈ 4,100 Europeans + 2,228 Asiatics + 684,284 counted natives + ~300,000 estimated uncounted natives ≈ 990,000-1,000,000, essentially matching the FAO 1952 'New Guinea' population figure of 1,006,000 (1000 people) almost exactly. Papua's population was reported separately (~300,000, much smaller), so the FAO 'New Guinea' label is NOT a combined Papua+New Guinea figure — it refers specifically to the Mandated Territory of New Guinea, i.e. candidate TNGU-1920-1949's own territory. The neighbor_segments field shows 1950-1951 correctly routed to PNG-1949-1975 (the post-merger successor polity), consistent with the 1949-07-01 administrative union documented on the wiki page. The observed span (1937-1949) falls entirely within TNGU's 1920-1949 existence and its colonial boundary (former German New Guinea, CShapes area 237,536 km²) did not change during this span (Japanese occupation 1942-45 was a wartime occupation, not a redrawing of the administrative unit, and Australian civil administration resumed with the same boundaries in 1945). Wiki page is draft and its content is essentially a restatement of this same routing decision (circular if relied on alone), so the confirm here rests on the independently-verified population magnitude match, not the page.
verdict.wiki_note: External corroboration for the FAO 1952 'New Guinea' routing: 1941 Australian administrative population figures for the Territory of New Guinea alone (≈990k-1M, excluding Papua's separately-reported ~300k) closely match the FAO 1952 population magnitude (1,006,000), confirming the label denotes the Mandated Territory only, not a combined Papua+New Guinea figure.

review.basis: FAO 1952 "New Guinea" 1937-1949 data (6 rows, population median 1,006,000; copra ~62k tonnes) was routed to TNGU-1920-1949 (Territory of New Guinea, the Australian-administered League of Nations mandate, area 237,536 km², distinct from the separately-administered Territory of Papua until their 1949 merger into PNG-1949-1975). Web research found the Territory of New Guinea's actual 1941 population was ~990,612 (4,100 Europeans + 2,228 Asiatics + 684,284 counted natives + ~300,000 estimated uncounted natives), administered wholly separately from Papua (which had its own ~300,000-plus population reported under its own administration). The FAO figure of 1,006,000 sits within ~1.5% of this independently sourced 1941 total, strongly corroborating that the source's "New Guinea" label denotes the Mandated Territory alone, not a Papua+New Guinea combination — ruling out both the sub-territory fold-up and combined-reporting failure modes. The candidate's own wiki page is a thin, unreviewed draft that only restates the routing decision (circular), but the neighbor segment shows 1950-1951 correctly rerouted to PNG-1949-1975 exactly at the real 1949 administrative union date, which is independently consistent with known history and supports that the period split and routing logic here are sound.
review.wiki_note: Independent corroboration: Territory of New Guinea's actual 1941 population was ~990,600 (4,100 Europeans, 2,228 Asiatics, 684,284 counted + ~300,000 estimated uncounted natives), administered entirely separately from Territory of Papua (~300k+ pop, own administration) until their 1949 union. FAO 1952's "New Guinea" 1937-1949 population median of 1,006,000 matches this mandate-only total within ~1.5%, confirming the label is NOT a Papua+New Guinea combination. Worth adding to the page, which currently only states the routing decision without independent sourcing.

verdict.basis: The assertion covers Guam livestock/agriculture data (cattle, poultry, tractors, goats, buffaloes) for 1937-1950, routed to GUM-1898-1950 (Territory of Guam, 550 km², US unincorporated territory since the 1898 Treaty of Paris cession). Guam is a single small island with no sub-national splits, no union/empire scope ambiguity, and no annexation/cession events during 1937-1950 (Japanese occupation 1941-1944 is a wartime interruption, not a change in the territory the label denotes, and likely explains the sparse n=2-6 per staple across only 4 distinct years rather than any scope change). The staple magnitudes (cattle median 4k head, poultry 36k, pigs 8k, a handful of tractors) are all plausible for a 550 km² island and show no discontinuity suggesting a broader or narrower reporting scope. The wiki page, though draft/thin, states facts (cession 1898, Navy administration until 1950 Organic Act, GUM-1950-2025 successor) that are uncontested historical record and consistent with the routing; I did not need to rely on any territorial claim beyond these well-known facts. Neighbor segment 1951-1951 correctly maps to the successor polity GUM-1950-2025, confirming period boundaries are handled correctly at the edge. No indication of combined reporting, boundary-vintage mismatch, or sub-territory fold-up.

Assertion iraq|mitchell|1923-1931 routes Mitchell's "iraq" agricultural series (wheat, barley, tobacco) for years 1923-1931 to candidate IRQ-1921-1932 (British Mandate for Mesopotamia) via ISO match. The candidate's wiki page is draft status (unreviewed prior-agent hypothesis), so I treated its claims as a hypothesis rather than evidence, but its core factual claim — that Iraq under British Mandate used the 1932 independence-era borders as a polygon proxy because no earlier polygon exists, with the Mosul vilayet dispute (1922-1925) not actually changing effective British administrative control — matches independently known history: Mosul was administered by Britain/Iraq throughout the mandate despite Turkey's international claim, with the League of Nations formally awarding it to Iraq in 1925/ratified 1926. So the reporting territory (the whole mandate, including Mosul) was constant for the entire observed span 1923-1931, which sits fully inside the candidate's 1921-1932 period. The magnitudes (wheat ~350,000 t, barley ~603,000 ha, tobacco ~6,300 t) are plausible for 1920s Iraqi agricultural output at national scale, no discontinuity suggested. The neighbor segment 1932-1960 routes cleanly to the successor IRQ-1932-2025 (same ISO/territory, per CShapes proxy), consistent with the mandate/independence pair sharing identical borders (both use polygon_feature_year 1932). No sub-territory fold-up concern since "Iraq" here is the whole national reporting unit, not a province label. No combined-reporting risk (Iraq wasn't merged with another mandate for Mitchell's purposes). Verdict: confirm, verified_equal, since territory is both equal to the candidate and constant across the whole observed span.

review.basis: Iraq (British Mandate for Mesopotamia), IRQ-1921-1932, is a single national-level polity in the DB with clean start/end boundaries (1921-1932) and a direct successor (IRQ-1932-2025) covering the same territory post-independence. The Mosul vilayet sovereignty dispute (1922-1925) was between Britain/Iraq and Turkey but Mosul was administered by British/Iraqi authorities throughout, so it was part of the reporting/administered territory the whole time — no sub-territory fold-up or combined-reporting issue applies. verdict.basis: The assertion covers FAO 1952's 'Libya' label for 1950-1951, which exactly matches the candidate LBY-1950-1951's declared period (1950-1951), a short bridging polity representing all-Libya (Tripolitania+Cyrenaica+Fezzan) under UN Transitional Administration before the December 1951 independence of the unified Kingdom of Libya.
